audience: Engineers who know API and database basics and that requests can execute simultaneously, but do not know vendor-specific key-value APIs. Explain mechanisms and limits in plain English.
prerequisites: An API handler can read and write records in a database.
Several requests can execute at the same time and affect shared data.
A network request may fail to return a response.

objectives.description: Explain key-value access as looking up a value by its key, and distinguish that access model from a cache role or a durability guarantee.
Trace basic get, put and delete operations while distinguishing an absent key from an operation whose result is unknown because it failed.
Choose a value boundary and unambiguous key identity that match a lookup, while separating key namespaces from permission checks.
Explain why direct lookup by known key does not automatically support queries on value fields, and compare a scan with a maintained index.
Trace a lost update from read-modify-write and explain how an atomic conditional write can detect the conflict.
Explain why an uncertain write may already have taken effect and distinguish retries that repeat an effect from those that leave the same state.
Distinguish TTL expiration from capacity eviction and explain why removal rules do not guarantee retention, refresh or timed business execution.
Explain how distributing groups of keys can spread work but leave a hot key, and distinguish read consistency from durability when evaluating guarantees.
Choose whether key-value access fits a workload by weighing known-key operations against query needs and required correctness guarantees.

questions.question: A service stores each tenant's device settings as its authoritative record and looks up the complete settings by tenant and device ID. Device IDs repeat across tenants, and the store also holds device-status records. Explain the key-value model, propose an unambiguous key and value for this lookup, and explain why this use need not be a cache or inherently durable. Under an example API where put replaces the whole value, trace put {mode: quiet, color: green}, then put {mode: loud}, then get, delete and get on that key. Distinguish the confirmed absent result from a get timeout, and explain why possession of the key does not grant permission to read it.
criteria: Explains lookup by a known key, uses tenant/device/record-kind identity, and chooses the settings read together as the value.
Distinguishes the authoritative-record role from a disposable cache copy and requires checking actual durability rather than inferring it from the access model.
The first get returns only {mode: loud}; the get after delete reports absent under the specified API.
A timed-out get leaves the result unknown and is not evidence of absence.
Key namespaces prevent identity collisions; the service still checks caller authorization.
criticalMisconceptions: All key-value data is a disposable cache.
Timeout and absence are equivalent.
Key names provide authorization.

questions.question: Equipment records are directly retrievable by equipment ID, but a new request asks for every record with region = west without supplying IDs. Explain why basic key lookup alone cannot discover the matches, compare a scan with an index from region to IDs, and explain both how their read work differs and what extra update responsibility the index introduces. Can the team assume that every key-value store provides such an index?
criteria: The region field is not the known equipment key, so direct lookup alone does not discover matching records.
A scan inspects entries and filters values, with work growing with the entries inspected.
An index identifies matching IDs and can avoid scanning every value, but must be maintained when records or regions change.
Index support and guarantees must be checked in the selected store.
criticalMisconceptions: Fields stored inside values automatically have query indexes.
Indexes impose no update responsibility.

questions.question: Two workers read a stored count of 20 with version 7. Both intend to add one, and each blindly writes 21. Explain the result and the lost update. An alternative implementation offers an atomic conditional put that succeeds only when the stored version matches and changes the version on success. Trace how that prevents the two stale writes from both succeeding, describe how the rejected worker preserves its increment, and explain why a separate check followed by an unconditional put would not provide the same protection.
criteria: Blind writes leave 21 instead of 22 because both increments were computed from the same old value.
An indivisible condition-and-write lets only one write using version 7 succeed.
The rejected worker rereads and recomputes against the current value and version before another conditional attempt.
A separate check and unconditional put allows a concurrent change in between and therefore does not close the race.
criticalMisconceptions: Atomic individual writes make read-modify-write sequences automatically safe.
A separate version check eliminates the race.

questions.question: An operation times out after sending a request. Compare retrying an identical replacement put when no other write intervenes with retrying an operation that adds one each time it runs. Explain what the timeout leaves unknown, the effect of each retry and what would be needed to avoid a duplicate increment. The same store advertises TTL expiration and capacity eviction. Distinguish those removal triggers and explain whether the TTL promises retention until its deadline, a refreshed value after removal, or a business action at the exact deadline. State which of these behaviors must be checked for the chosen product and configuration.
criteria: A missing response does not reveal whether the first write took effect.
An identical replacement put has the same final value under the specified assumption; repeating an increment can apply its effect twice.
A duplicate increment needs prevention through a verified mechanism recognizing the same logical operation, or avoidance of a blind retry; no universal store feature is assumed.
Expiration is based on an entry lifetime rule; capacity eviction may remove it earlier.
TTL does not by itself guarantee retention, refresh or exact-time business execution.
Retry semantics, any duplicate prevention, and lifetime or eviction behavior depend on the actual implementation and configuration.
criticalMisconceptions: A timeout proves failure to execute.
TTL guarantees exact-time business execution or retention.

questions.question: Explain what a data partition means in a store that distributes groups of keys across nodes. Most requests now target one key. Explain how distribution helps many-key workloads and why more partitions alone may not fix this hot key. After a successful write, a read from a lagging copy returns an older value. Explain the consistency issue, distinguish it from durability after a failure, and say what must be verified before promising latest-value reads or survival of acknowledged writes.
criteria: Defines a data partition as a portion of keyspace assigned to a node or group, without assuming prior sharding knowledge.
Different key groups can spread work, while demand for a single key can remain concentrated on its serving capacity.
Read consistency describes what writes a read is guaranteed to observe; a lagging copy may serve old data if the selected behavior permits it.
Durability concerns survival of acknowledged data under specified failures, not whether a reader immediately sees it.
The chosen implementation, configuration and operation mode determine these guarantees; the key-value label or node count does not.
criticalMisconceptions: More partitions necessarily spread one key across all available capacity.
Acknowledgment alone establishes all read-visibility and failure-survival guarantees.

questions.question: Service A gets and replaces independent preferences by a known account key. Service B needs frequent joins across records and changing filters on their fields. Compare their fit for basic key-value access, explaining the benefit for A and a concrete cost for B. For A, choose two correctness or capacity requirements from this lesson that you would verify before selecting a store, and explain why each matters. Can you conclude from the access model alone that the service will be fast and safe?
criteria: A aligns with retrieving a value by a known key; B needs access beyond that basic operation.
Explains a cost of supporting B through scans, maintained indexes, duplicated data or application coordination.
Selects and explains two relevant checks for A such as authorization, atomic updates, safe retries, consistency, durability, retention or hot-key capacity.
Rejects universal speed or safety guarantees from the model alone and ties the decision to actual requirements and implementation.
criticalMisconceptions: Key-value access is always the best or fastest choice.
Known-key access eliminates the need to verify correctness guarantees.

cards.objective: Explain key-value access as looking up a value by its key, and distinguish that access model from a cache role or a durability guarantee.

questions.question: One service keeps its only copy of a settings record in a store addressed by account ID. Another keeps a disposable copy of a computed page in a store addressed by page ID. Explain the key and value in each case, what makes both uses key-value access, and which is a cache role. Does the key-value label alone establish that the settings survive a store failure?
criteria: Identifies the account or page identifier as the key and the settings record or computed page as its associated value.
Explains that the caller uses a known key to retrieve its associated value in both cases.
Distinguishes the disposable reusable copy as a cache role from the only-copy data use; key-value access can serve either role.
Says durability requires checking the storage implementation and configuration, not inferring it from the access model.
criticalMisconceptions: Every key-value store is necessarily a disposable cache.
The key-value label alone guarantees durable storage.

cards.objective: Trace basic get, put and delete operations while distinguishing an absent key from an operation whose result is unknown because it failed.

questions.question: For this example, put replaces the entire value at a key, get returns either its value or an absent result, and delete removes the entry. All of these operations succeed in order: put K with {name: A, color: blue}; put K with {name: B}; get K; delete K; get K. Trace the two get results. Separately, a get of K times out without a response. What does that timeout establish about whether K exists, and should the handler report the same result as a confirmed absent key?
criteria: The first get returns {name: B}; the earlier color field is not retained under the specified replacement behavior.
The get after delete reports absent.
A timeout does not establish presence or absence because no result was obtained.
The handler preserves the distinction between confirmed absence and an operational failure or unknown result.
criticalMisconceptions: A replacement put automatically merges fields.
A timeout proves that the key is absent.

cards.objective: Choose a value boundary and unambiguous key identity that match a lookup, while separating key namespaces from permission checks.

questions.question: A service reads a complete device-preferences record by tenant ID and device ID. Different tenants can reuse device IDs, and the same store also contains device-status records. Propose a key and value for the preferences lookup, explain how they prevent identity collisions and match what the caller reads, and explain whether a caller who guesses that key should automatically receive the value.
criteria: The key unambiguously distinguishes tenant, device and record kind; any clear representation is accepted.
The value contains the preferences read together by this lookup, with a boundary matching that access pattern.
Explains why device ID alone or omitting record kind can select another record.
Explains that namespacing distinguishes identities but access control must still check the caller permission before returning data.
criticalMisconceptions: A device-only key isolates tenants that reuse IDs.
A namespace or difficult-to-guess key is sufficient authorization.

cards.objective: Explain why direct lookup by known key does not automatically support queries on value fields, and compare a scan with a maintained index.

questions.question: A store provides direct lookup by asset ID, and each value contains a city field. A new endpoint needs all assets in one city, but callers do not know their IDs. Explain why existing key lookups alone do not answer this request, how a scan could find matches and why its work grows, and how an index from city to asset IDs could help. Name the extra responsibility that index adds when an asset changes city, and state what must be checked before assuming the store provides the index.
criteria: A city value is not the known asset key; direct key lookup alone cannot discover all matching keys.
A scan examines stored entries and filters their values, so work grows with the entries examined rather than only the matching results.
An index maps city to relevant asset IDs so those values can be fetched without inspecting every value.
The index must be maintained as records change, adding update work and a consistency responsibility.
Index availability and behavior are implementation-specific, not inherent in every key-value store.
criticalMisconceptions: Putting a field in a value automatically creates an efficient query on that field.
An additional index requires no maintenance when data changes.

cards.objective: Trace a lost update from read-modify-write and explain how an atomic conditional write can detect the conflict.

questions.question: Two requests both read a counter value of 10 with version 4. Each adds one locally and blindly puts 11. Explain the final value and the lost update. Suppose this implementation supports an atomic put only if the stored version still matches the version read, and changes the version on success. Explain what happens to the two writes, how the rejected request can preserve its intended increment, and why a separate version check followed by an unconditional put is insufficient.
criteria: Both blind writes store 11, so one of the two intended increments is lost.
An atomic conditional write tests the version and writes as one indivisible operation; only one write based on version 4 succeeds.
The rejected request reads the current value and version, recomputes its increment and attempts a new conditional write rather than overwriting with the stale value.
A separate check and put leaves a gap in which another request can change the value.
criticalMisconceptions: Each individually successful get and put makes the full read-modify-write sequence atomic.
Checking a version separately from an unconditional write prevents lost updates.

cards.objective: Explain why an uncertain write may already have taken effect and distinguish retries that repeat an effect from those that leave the same state.

questions.question: A write times out after being sent, so the caller has no response. Compare blindly retrying a put of exactly the same value, with no intervening writes, to retrying an increment operation that adds one on each execution. Explain what is unknown and why the effects differ. Name a condition that would make increment retries safe against duplicate effects, or a safe policy when that condition cannot be established. Explain what must be verified before relying on that behavior in a chosen store.
criteria: The timeout leaves execution unknown: the first operation may have completed despite the missing response.
Repeating the same replacement put under the stated no-intervening-write assumption leaves the same stored value, while repeating an increment can add twice.
Safe increment retries require a verified mechanism that recognizes the same logical operation and prevents a second effect, or a policy that does not blindly repeat the uncertain increment.
The actual operation semantics and duplicate-effect protection must be verified in the implementation; individual atomicity does not by itself make retries harmless.
criticalMisconceptions: A timeout proves that a write did not happen.
Every retry is harmless because individual writes are atomic.

cards.objective: Distinguish TTL expiration from capacity eviction and explain why removal rules do not guarantee retention, refresh or timed business execution.

questions.question: A store supports TTL expiration and may evict entries under memory pressure. Explain the two removal triggers. Does a TTL guarantee that an entry remains until its deadline? Does expiration or eviction fetch a fresh replacement or prove that a business action ran at the exact deadline? Explain why support, eviction settings and when reads stop returning expired values must be checked before relying on a selected product and configuration.
criteria: Expiration follows an entry lifetime rule; eviction removes entries to manage capacity, potentially before the TTL.
A TTL does not guarantee retention until the deadline when other removal causes are possible.
Removal does not by itself refresh data or execute a business action at an exact time.
TTL support and expiry behavior, including when reads stop returning expired values, and eviction settings depend on the implementation and configuration.
criticalMisconceptions: A TTL guarantees retention until its deadline.
Removing an entry automatically refreshes it or runs business work exactly then.

cards.objective: Explain how distributing groups of keys can spread work but leave a hot key, and distinguish read consistency from durability when evaluating guarantees.

questions.question: Define a data partition as used when distributing keys across storage nodes. A store distributes many keys across such partitions, but 80% of requests ask for one key. Explain why adding partitions may not remove that bottleneck. Separately, an acknowledged write may be followed by a read from a copy that has not caught up. Explain the read-consistency concern, distinguish it from whether the write survives a failure, and identify what must be checked before relying on either guarantee. No consensus algorithm or partition-routing algorithm is required.
criteria: Defines a data partition as a portion of the keyspace assigned to a storage node or group, explaining the term locally.
Distributing different keys can spread load, but requests to one hot key may still concentrate on its serving capacity.
The read-consistency question concerns which completed writes a read is guaranteed to observe; a lagging copy can return an older value when the selected mode permits it.
Durability concerns whether acknowledged data survives specified failures, which is distinct from read visibility.
Both guarantees depend on the chosen implementation, configuration and operation mode; neither follows just from using key-value access or multiple nodes.
criticalMisconceptions: More partitions automatically divide all work for a single hot key.
An acknowledged write means every later read from any copy sees it and it survives every failure.

cards.objective: Choose whether key-value access fits a workload by weighing known-key operations against query needs and required correctness guarantees.

questions.question: Compare two services: A retrieves and replaces one independent device-settings record using a known tenant/device identity; B frequently joins customer and order records and asks changing filters over their fields. Which is the more direct fit for basic key-value access, and why? Explain a cost of forcing B into that access model, and identify two requirements you would verify before choosing a particular store for A, explaining why each matters. Does either the workload fit or the key-value label prove a performance or safety guarantee?
criteria: A is the more direct fit because its unit of access is a record selected by a known key.
B requires access beyond a known key; forcing it into basic key-value access adds scans, maintained indexes, duplicated data or application coordination, with an explained cost.
Identifies and explains two relevant requirements for A, such as access isolation, concurrency protection, retry behavior, read consistency, durability, retention or hot-key capacity.
Workload fit and the access-model label do not prove performance or safety; the actual implementation and workload must support those requirements.
criticalMisconceptions: Key-value stores are always faster for every workload.
Known-key access alone guarantees safe concurrent updates or durable writes.
